_comment: bb-auth settings file — TEMPLATE. The real one is <install-dir>/var/lib/settings.json,
created by the package and never shipped, exactly like access.json: it is state.
What is in here and what is not is decided by one rule. A setting lives in this file
iff it (1) is read per request, so a new value takes effect on the next one, (2) cannot
lock the operator out irreversibly, and (3) is not a secret. What is left in bb-auth.env
is the listener, the worker count, the HMAC key, the cookie's NAME, the path of the
access file, and BB_AUTH_ORIGINAL_URL_HEADER.
THE WHOLE COGNITO WIRING IS HERE, the pool included: gate.issuer is the user pool whose
iss and signing keys every id_token is checked against, gate.client_id is the app client
the email flow uses, and each gate.social_buttons audience is the app client that
federates that provider. The app clients ARE the accepted audiences.
SO IS THE ESTATE: gate.cookie_domain and gate.authorized_hosts, which are checked
against each other, because a host the cookie cannot reach is a login that lands, sends
no cookie, gets a 401 and bounces back to the sign-in page for ever, with nothing
anywhere saying why.
FIVE OF THESE CAN STOP PEOPLE GETTING IN: issuer, client_id, login_url, cookie_domain,
and taking a host off authorized_hosts. Both editors ask before writing one (`--yes` on
bb-auth-adm, a panel and a second click in bb-auth-web), and asking is enough rather
than refusing because none of them invalidates a cookie: whoever makes the edit still
holds a session and can undo it. It is five and not fifteen on purpose, since a
confirmation that fires on every save is a button people learn to click without
reading.
It is a file rather than more env vars for one mechanical reason: a process cannot
re-read its own environment. systemd loads EnvironmentFile= once, at ExecStart, so
nothing in an env file can ever be reloaded without a restart.
Edit it with `bb-auth-adm settings ...`, or from bb-auth-web's Settings tab; both go
through the same validate-before-write. Check one by hand with:
bb-auth --check-settings settings.json
The gate re-reads it on SIGHUP (systemctl reload bb-auth) and a file it refuses leaves
the running values in place; bb-auth-web reads it fresh on every request.
COMMENTS LIVE UP HERE, and that is not a limitation to work around: unknown keys inside
a section are a hard error, for the reason a misspelled scope field is one. A setting
silently dropped is worse than a setting refused. Unknown keys at THIS level are kept
across an edit, which is what makes these blocks survive a save from either editor.
_comment_profile_claims: gate.profile_claims — OIDC claims to hand to the application on a 204, in the order the
headers come out. EMPTY BY DEFAULT: nothing is propagated but the identity.
The header name is DERIVED and never configured: '_' and ':' become '-', each part is
title-cased, and 'X-Auth-' is prefixed. given_name -> X-Auth-Given-Name,
$upstream_http_x_auth_custom_department). A claim name may contain only [A-Za-z0-9_:-];
anything else, a claim the gate consumes itself (email, email_verified, token_use,
identities), or two entries deriving the same header, is refused rather than skipped.
These are self-asserted profile attributes: display hints, never authorization. They
ride inside the session cookie, so keep the list short (a browser silently drops a
cookie over ~4 KB, and the gate warns at startup when you get close). Changing it is NOT
a cookie-format change: nobody is logged out, a claim removed stops being emitted at
once, and one added appears at each user's next sign-in.
_comment_identity_attrs: gate.identity_attrs — which identity attributes a 204 names. Default ['email'], which is
what every application behind the gate already reads. Only 'email' and 'uuid' exist; a
third would be a code change, not a string you may invent. An empty list is refused: a
204 that names nobody breaks every application behind the gate, in silence.
NGINX MUST CLEAR EVERY POSSIBLE NAME, not the ones enabled here. proxy_set_header
overrides only the names it lists, so a header you neither set nor clear is one a client
can send. Clear X-Auth-Uuid on every gated location even while it is off, and turning it
on here later needs no nginx change at all.
Multiple values of one attribute come out SPACE-separated (a user with two emails); a
space can never appear inside an identifier, which is what makes that unambiguous.
_comment_social: gate.allow_unverified_social — relax the email_verified requirement, but ONLY for
federated (social) logins. Cognito cannot verify the email of a Google/Apple sign-up, so
it stamps email_verified=false even though the IdP asserted the address. Native
self-signup stays strict: an unverified native email is attacker-controlled. It
multiplies with an 'authenticated' scope: together they mean any social account,
gate.social_providers narrows it to named IdPs, matched case-insensitively against the
token's identities[].providerName. Empty = any federated provider. Prefer listing only
_comment_issuer: gate.issuer — the Cognito USER POOL this deployment trusts: the value every id_token's
`iss` must equal, and the host its JWKS is fetched from. Absolute https, no trailing
slash. EMPTY MEANS NO TOKEN CAN BE VALIDATED, which is the state a fresh install is in;
the gate starts anyway and says so loudly, because a package creates this file and
cannot know the value. Set the first one with `bb-auth-adm settings set --issuer ...`
over SSH: bb-auth-web is itself behind the gate, so on a fresh install there is no
It is the one setting here that is NOT read per request: it is read once, to fetch the
signing keys. The reload pays for that, and pays for it atomically: a SIGHUP that sees a
new pool fetches its JWKS first and swaps the keys and the settings together or swaps
neither, because a gate holding half of that pair checks one pool's tokens against the
_comment_cookie_domain: gate.cookie_domain — the session cookie's Domain, with or without the leading dot RFC
6265 ignores. EMPTY is a host-only cookie, which only serves a deployment where the gate
and the application are one host; a parent domain (.example.com) is what makes one login
cover every service behind the gate.
CHANGING IT DOES NOT LOG ANYBODY OUT, AND THAT IS THE PROBLEM. A browser matches a
clearing Set-Cookie on (name, Domain, Path), so every cookie already issued under the old
domain stays valid for its full lifetime AND /auth/logout can no longer clear it: a
logout that silently succeeds at nothing, for everybody who signed in before the edit.
The way back is to put the old value back, which makes those cookies clearable again.
_comment_authorized_hosts: gate.authorized_hosts — the hosts a post-login `rd` may land on, as host globs. The ONLY
authority on where a redirect may go. There is no 'service base URL': one gate fronts
several hosts and which one is in play is decided by the caller.
Same wildcards a scope's urls use: `*` = any run of characters, `&` = exactly one.
`*.example.com` does NOT match the bare apex, so list it too if you want it.
EMPTY REFUSES EVERY REDIRECT TARGET THERE IS, so every login lands on the sign-in page
instead of where the visitor was going: useless, fail-closed, and tolerated for the
Every entry must be reachable by cookie_domain above, or this file is refused.
_comment_client_id: gate.client_id — the Cognito APP CLIENT the email flow uses: the one the sign-in page
runs USER_AUTH against, and the first audience a token is accepted for. EMPTY MEANS NO
LOGIN CAN COMPLETE, which is the state a fresh install is in; the gate starts anyway and
says so at startup, because a package creates this file and cannot know the value.
It is the one setting here that can stop NEW logins. It cannot invalidate a cookie, so
whoever gets it wrong still holds their session and can undo it, and `bb-auth-adm` over
SSH is the way back if not.
_comment_login_url: gate.login_url — where people sign in: the page a 401 names for nginx to redirect to,
and the page a rejected redirect target falls back to. EMPTY MEANS the gate's own
/auth/login, on whatever host the request arrived at, which is what a deployment that
has not moved its sign-in page wants. Absolute https when it is set.
An application in the access file may override it for its own area (login_url there).
Whatever it names, nginx must leave /auth/login and /auth/callback UNGATED.
_comment_social_wiring: gate.oauth_domain / gate.social_callback_url — the Cognito hosted UI this deployment
sends people to, as a bare host, and the redirect_uri it comes back to. Empty means no
social sign-in at all. The callback URL must be registered BYTE FOR BYTE on every app
client named below, which is Amazon's rule: get it wrong and whoever clicks a button is
told redirect_mismatch, in Amazon's words, on Amazon's page.
_comment_social_buttons: gate.social_buttons — which social buttons the sign-in page OFFERS, in the order they
appear, and THE APP CLIENT EACH ONE RUNS THROUGH. EMPTY OFFERS NONE: a provider is shown
because somebody wrote it here, never because the deployment happens to federate it.
Changing it takes effect on the next request, with no restart.
Each entry is { "idp": <Cognito identity_provider>, "audience": <app client id> }. The
app client is per button because Cognito federates per app client: which providers a
client offers is a property of that client, so two providers may live on two of them and
one value for all of them could not say so. A bare name, which is what this list held
before, is refused with a sentence rather than a type error.
It is a different question from social_providers above: that one decides whose
unverified email is accepted, this one what a visitor is shown.
_comment_session_ttl_secs: gate.session_ttl_secs — the session cookie's lifetime, in seconds. Applies to cookies
minted from now on and to no cookie already in a browser, so changing it logs nobody
out. Below 60s is refused (a session that expires as it is handed over is a login loop);
above 400 days is warned about, because that is the cap browsers apply to Max-Age
regardless of what the header says.
_comment_admins: web.admins — who may use bb-auth-web, matched against the X-Auth-Email nginx injects
(trimmed and lowercased, so a login's capitalisation cannot matter). REQUIRED and never
empty: bb-auth-web refuses to serve without one, and both editors refuse to write an
empty list. The gate ignores this section entirely.
It is deliberate defense in depth, not a second copy of the roster: a scope that grants
on identity alone (anonymous or authenticated) covering the admin URL would otherwise
hand the admin surface to any Cognito account, and self-signup is open. But it is the
BACKSTOP, not the lock: the gate is what stands in front, so the admin area must be a
'restricted' scope that lists each admin, and covered by NO anonymous or authenticated
The GUI will not let an administrator remove themselves from this list. That is on
purpose, and `bb-auth-adm settings admin rm` is the way to do it anyway.
_comment_ui: ui — how every page BOTH programs serve looks: the gate's sign-in page, its social
callback and its error page, and the whole bb-auth-web GUI. It is the one section they
share, and it passes the three-part rule above the way the rest do: read when a page is
rendered, harmless when wrong (an unstyled page, never a locked door), no secret.
stylesheet_url — a stylesheet loaded AFTER the built-in one, so it wins by source order
and needs no !important. Either an absolute https:// URL or a path starting with / on
this host. It is meant to redefine the theme's custom properties (--bg, --card, --text,
--accent, --r-box, --font-ui …) and nothing else: that is what lets ONE file restyle the
sign-in page and the admin GUI together, knowing nothing about either layout. Both
binaries carry a complete stylesheet already, so leaving this empty is a fully styled
deployment, and a URL that does not answer costs a page its palette and nothing more.
A sign-in page must never NEED a second host to be up.
logo_url — shown on the sign-in page above the name. Same two shapes. Empty = the name
brand_name — what the sign-in page calls this deployment. Empty = each page's own name.
theme — system (default), light or dark: which arm of the palette a page starts in. The
gate's pages have nowhere to keep a per-visitor choice, so for them this is the whole
